title: How to Extract a Design System from an Existing Website
description: Audit colors, typography, spacing, and component states on a live website. Build a useful token inventory while separating observations from assumptions.
body:
To extract a design system from a website, inspect representative pages, record recurring styles, group those observations into named tokens, and verify them across components and states. The result is a reconstructed inventory. A live website alone cannot tell you all of the team’s original design decisions, component APIs, or unpublished guidelines.

Start with one useful deliverable: a token sheet plus a few component specifications. You can expand it once you know which rules repeat. Trying to collect every CSS declaration first usually produces more cleanup than insight.

Choose a representative sample

Select pages that exercise different layouts: a marketing page, an article or documentation page, a form, and a list or dashboard if one exists. Within each, inspect a heading, paragraph, link, button, field, card, and navigation item. Record unavailable components as missing evidence, not as invented styles.

Set a clear scope: the viewport, theme, signed-in state, and date. If you have only a homepage, say so. A homepage can provide a visual direction, but it is a weak basis for claiming a complete product design system.

Build an observation inventory

CategoryRecordCheck again on
ColorsValue, alpha, role, paired backgroundText, buttons, alerts, menus
TypographyRendered family, weight, size, line heightHeadings, body, labels, forms
SpacingGap, padding, margin, container widthCards, sections, compact layouts
ShapeBorder widths, radii, shadowsButtons, cards, dialogs
BehaviorFocus, hover, error, disabled statesKeyboard and pointer interaction

Use the dedicated font identification and color palette extraction guides for those passes. Keeping each pass focused makes it easier to compare the same property across several components.

Separate observations from inferred rules

Imagine observing card padding of 16px, 24px, and 32px. You might propose an 8px spacing step, but those three observations do not prove the entire site follows it. A 20px button inset or a fluid section gap could be equally intentional.

Keep two columns: observed value and proposed token. Add a confidence note based on repeated evidence. This is an editorial working method, not a statistical score. For example:

Observation: 24px gap between cards on the listing page
Proposal: space.section-item = 24px
Evidence: repeated in two desktop lists
Open question: mobile list uses a different gap
Decision: keep responsive values separate for now

This record gives the next person a reason for the choice and a way to challenge it. A token name without evidence can turn a guess into a rule that nobody remembers making.

Turn repeated values into meaningful tokens

Separate raw values from intended roles. A raw color might be green.200; a role might be color.action.background. Components should use roles where the meaning is stable. Avoid a token named after a particular position, such as left-card-green, unless that location is the real design concept.

The Design Tokens Community Group format defines a JSON interchange structure with token types, values, and aliases. It is useful when tools need to exchange tokens; it does not automatically reconstruct component behavior from a rendered page.

For a smaller project, a reviewed CSS variable file may be sufficient. MDN’s custom properties guide explains how values can be referenced and scoped. Choose the export format your project will actually maintain.

Write component specifications alongside the tokens

A button needs more than a background token. Document its label style, horizontal and vertical padding, border, minimum dimensions, focus appearance, disabled treatment, and behavior with a long label. Note which details you observed and which you are choosing for your own implementation.

Use a deliberately small validation set: one button, one form field, one card, and a page header. Rebuild them with your token sheet, then compare at narrow and wide widths. When they diverge, inspect the rule responsible instead of adding unexplained magic numbers.

Our CSS inspection guide covers the difference between a declaration in a stylesheet and the resolved styles you see. That distinction matters when a flexible layout produces a pixel width that should not become a fixed token.

Make the handoff usable

Deliver the source URLs and capture conditions, the named token file, component notes, unresolved questions, and a short list of permitted assets. Keep proprietary logos, font files, and illustrations out of a redistribution bundle unless you have the rights to include them.

For Tailwind projects, continue with mapping the inventory into Tailwind v4. For an AI coding workflow, use the DESIGN.md template to explain the decisions and explicitly instruct your agent to read it. A good handoff preserves uncertainty and rationale as carefully as it preserves hex codes.
imageAlt: A website reference connects to four reusable design-system layers: color, typography, spacing and shape.
coverAlt: A light design token inspector with accent color, card radius, typography and shadow values.

title: How to Find the Font on a Website in Chrome
description: Identify a website’s real rendered font, size, weight, and line height in Chrome. Learn why font stacks and screenshot guesses can mislead you.
keyword: how to find font on website
body:
To find the font on a website, right-click the text, choose Inspect, and open Elements → Computed in Chrome DevTools. Check font-family, then scroll to Rendered Fonts to identify the typeface actually used. Record the size, weight, and line height too: the family name alone will not reproduce the typography.

This guide is for live, selectable website text. If the lettering is inside a photograph, screenshot, or outlined logo, you need image-based identification instead. Start by checking which kind of material you have.

Choose a method for the text you have

What you can accessStart hereWhat to verify
Selectable live textChrome’s element inspectorRendered font and computed styles
A screenshot or photoAn image-based font matching serviceCandidate matches, not an exact CSS declaration
A logo built with SVG pathsBrand guidelines or the original design fileWhether the lettering was customized
Your own source projectFont declarations and component stylesWhich files load in the browser

For example, a heading can look like ordinary text while sitting inside a hero image. Try selecting a word. If the browser selects the entire image instead, inspecting that image will not reveal the font used to create its pixels.

Inspect the exact text element

  1. Open the page and wait for its text to settle.
  2. Right-click the heading or paragraph you want, then choose Inspect.
  3. In Elements, select the smallest element containing that text. A nested span may have different styling from its parent.
  4. Open Computed and search for font. Note family, size, style, and weight.
  5. Clear the filter and inspect Rendered Fonts near the bottom of the panel.

Chrome documents the Rendered Fonts section in its font inspection example. That section helps distinguish a local font from a web font. If the interface differs in your Chrome version, look for the Computed panel within Elements.

Why the first font name may be wrong

A declaration such as font-family: "Studio Sans", Arial, sans-serif is a preference list. It does not prove that Studio Sans loaded. The browser may use a fallback, and different characters can come from different fonts. MDN’s font-family reference explains the ordered selection and character-level fallback.

Consider a card with English text followed by an emoji. Treat the emoji font as a separate observation, not evidence that the whole card uses it. Similarly, a page may use one family for headings and another for forms. Sample each role you intend to recreate.

Record a useful typography specimen

Use a short record like this original example when moving from inspection to implementation. These values are illustrative, not measurements of another website:

Role: card title
Sample: A calmer way to work
Rendered family: Inter
Weight: 600
Size: 24px
Line height: 30px
Letter spacing: -0.3px
Container width: 320px
State: desktop, default

The container width matters because it changes where a line wraps. A correct font inside the wrong width may look like a wrong font. Save the exact sample text, viewport, and the state of the component so you can repeat the comparison.

Download the typography audit worksheet and fill one row per role. If you are collecting more than type, use the website design-system audit to keep the measurements together.

Troubleshoot a font that still looks different

  • Wrong weight: compare the actual weight, not just a “bold” label in your editor.
  • Wrong line breaks: match text, width, font size, and letter spacing before changing the family.
  • Late loading: reload and watch whether the text changes after the initial render.
  • Different device: check the same page on the device where the mismatch occurs.
  • Different state: inspect the element after opening its menu or changing its tab.

When the computed value is surprising, trace the matching CSS rule and inherited styles. Our CSS inspection workflow explains how to find the declaration behind a visible result.

Turn the observation into your own type system

Choose a small set of text roles: page heading, section heading, paragraph, label, and code. Give each a deliberate size and spacing rule. You do not need to copy every one-off size found on the reference page; that often imports accidental inconsistencies into your own design.

Obtain font files from the creator or an authorized distributor and check the license before reuse. A font being downloadable by a browser is not evidence that you can redistribute it. Keep your inspection notes separate from the files you are licensed to ship.

For a wider visual handoff, combine this worksheet with the color palette extraction guide. The useful deliverable is a set of named text roles and verified styles, not a folder of unexplained font filenames.
imageAlt: A typography specimen shows the distinction between a declared font-family list and the font actually rendered by the browser.
coverAlt: Three Inter letter specimens with 56px, 18px and 14px labels and a row of font weights.

title: How to Extract a Website Color Palette That You Can Use
description: Find a website’s colors in Chrome, separate CSS values from screenshot samples, and turn the result into a named palette with contrast checks.
body:
To extract a website color palette, inspect the page’s CSS colors, group them by role, and record the foreground/background pairs used together. Chrome’s CSS Overview panel can help you collect page colors. Use the element inspector to confirm each important value before turning the collection into reusable variables.

A useful palette answers “which color goes where?” A long list of hex codes does not. This workflow produces a small palette for surfaces, text, borders, and actions, plus a record of the combinations that need checking.

Decide whether you need CSS values or sampled pixels

Use CSS inspection when you have access to a live page. Use an eyedropper when you are studying a screenshot, illustration, or visible composite. Keep those results labeled separately. Transparency, shadows, and gradients can make a sampled pixel differ from the underlying color declaration.

For example, white text at partial opacity over a dark panel has both a source color and a rendered appearance. Recording only the sampled gray loses the opacity rule. If the panel later changes, that flattened sample no longer describes the intended treatment.

Collect colors with Chrome CSS Overview

  1. Open the page in the theme and viewport you want to study.
  2. Open Chrome DevTools and its command menu.
  3. Search for Show CSS Overview and open that panel.
  4. Select Capture overview.
  5. Review the colors section, then inspect representative elements for the values you plan to keep.

Chrome’s CSS Overview documentation describes its page-level color and font summaries. Treat the capture as an inventory for that page, not proof that you have found every theme, state, or component on the site.

Capture again after opening a modal or switching a theme if those views matter. Record what changed. A green “success” message and a green brand button may share a value while serving different purposes.

Name colors by their jobs

Start with a small worksheet. The following palette is an original teaching example, not an extracted brand palette:

RoleExample valueWhere to inspect
Canvas#0B100CPage background
Surface#18221BCard or menu background
Text#F4F7F1Paragraph on canvas
Muted text#B7C1B9Secondary label on surface
Action#AEDFBBPrimary button
On action#102016Text inside that button

Do not merge colors solely because their hex values look close. First ask whether they represent the same role. Keep separate semantic names if two roles may need to change independently, even when their current values match.

Check combinations, not individual swatches

A color does not pass contrast on its own. Check the text against the surface it actually sits on. WCAG 2.2’s minimum text contrast criterion generally calls for at least 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text, with defined exceptions. Read the W3C explanation and large-text definition when applying those thresholds.

Chrome’s Color Picker reference describes its contrast controls. Check which contrast model your tool displays; an APCA result is not a WCAG 2.x ratio. For gradients or photographs, examine the backgrounds behind the text across its occupied area.

Keep a matrix of actual combinations: text on canvas, muted text on surface, button text on action, and focus indicator against adjacent colors. Do not label the whole interface accessible after checking only one button.

Export a small set of CSS variables

Here is a reusable starting point for the example palette. It deliberately uses role names so you can change the visual direction without rewriting every component:

:root {
  --canvas: #0b100c;
  --surface: #18221b;
  --text: #f4f7f1;
  --text-muted: #b7c1b9;
  --action: #aedfbb;
  --on-action: #102016;
}
.card { background: var(--surface); color: var(--text); }
.button { background: var(--action); color: var(--on-action); }

Download the example palette CSS or follow the Tailwind token mapping guide to use named values in utility classes.

Avoid the common extraction mistakes

  • Saving only a screenshot: retain CSS values and their roles when you can inspect them.
  • Flattening transparency: record alpha and the background behind it.
  • Ignoring states: inspect hover, focus, selected, and error states that belong in your design.
  • Collecting photo colors as UI tokens: keep editorial imagery separate from interface colors.
  • Copying without a purpose: choose a palette suited to your content and verify your own combinations.

Pair the palette with a typography audit, then place both in the wider design-system inventory. Your final file should tell a builder how to use each color and which combinations still require review.
imageAlt: Five example website colors are organized into background, surface, text, accent and border roles.
coverAlt: Blue, black, gray and light gray swatches with an example text pair and its calculated 8.78 to 1 contrast ratio.

title: How to Inspect CSS on a Website with Chrome DevTools
description: Find the CSS behind any page element, understand computed styles, and check layouts, hover states, and responsive behavior in Chrome DevTools.
body:
To inspect CSS on a website, right-click the element and choose Inspect. In Chrome DevTools, use Styles to trace the rules that affect it and Computed to check the resulting values. Then inspect the parent layout, interactive states, and narrower screens before treating those values as a reusable component.

A useful inspection answers a specific question: why does this card have this width, where does this text color come from, or what makes this button change on focus? Start with one question and follow the evidence. Copying every property usually gives you a larger pile of CSS without explaining the design.

1. Select the element that owns the appearance

Right-click directly on the visible text, border, or image you want to understand. Check the selected node in the Elements panel. A click on a label may select a nested span even though the surrounding button owns its background, border, and padding.

Move between that node and its parent while watching the page highlight. For a card, inspect the outer container for spacing, the heading for typography, and the image for cropping. Record which element owns each decision. That small distinction makes your eventual implementation easier to maintain.

2. Separate authored rules from computed values

The Styles panel includes matching rules, including declarations that lose in the cascade. Computed gives you the values applied to the selected element. Filter by a property such as color and follow its source when you need to understand an override. Chrome documents both panels in its CSS features reference.

For an original example, imagine these two rules in your own stylesheet:

.card { color: #24332a; padding: 1.5rem; }
.featured .card { color: #102317; }

A card inside a container with the featured class gets the second color. The first rule still matters because it supplies the padding. Copying only the last rule would lose part of the component; copying both without their context would preserve a dependency you may not want.

Also record the authored unit where useful. A displayed pixel value can be the current result of a relative unit, a variable, or a calculation. The result is evidence of this rendering, not a complete account of the original design decision. MDN describes this distinction in the getComputedStyle reference.

3. Inspect the parent layout and box model

When an element seems too wide or incorrectly positioned, move outward. Look for the parent’s display mode, available width, alignment, and gap before changing the child’s margin. A consistent gap between siblings often belongs to their shared container.

Use the box-model diagram to distinguish content size from padding, borders, and margins. With box-sizing: border-box, the declared width includes padding and borders. MDN’s box-sizing reference explains the sizing models. For grids, Chrome’s grid overlay exposes tracks and lines, helping you distinguish a layout rule from coincidental alignment.

4. Check hover, focus, and content changes

Use the :hov control in Styles to force a relevant pseudo-class, such as hover or focus. Inspect any changed color, outline, shadow, or transform. Then use the keyboard on the actual page: a forced visual state does not tell you whether the interaction is usable.

For your own component, replace a short label with a longer one and increase the content length. Does the button wrap gracefully? Does the card expand? Record behavior alongside measurements. “The card grows with its content” is more useful than carrying over a fixed height measured from one short paragraph.

5. Compare wide and narrow screens

Open the device toolbar and use a responsive viewport. Resize gradually so you can see when the layout changes instead of testing only one phone preset. Chrome’s device mode guide explains the controls and notes that simulation is an approximation of a real mobile device.

Compare the same element at both widths. Record changes to columns, horizontal padding, text wrapping, and navigation. If you see a media query in Styles, keep its condition with your notes. If the layout simply flows into available space, avoid inventing a breakpoint that the evidence does not support.

6. Rebuild the smallest useful example

Turn the observations into a small component in your own project. Here is an original starting point for a flexible card, using deliberate example values rather than a copied site’s stylesheet:

.card {
  box-sizing: border-box;
  width: min(100%, 36rem);
  padding: 1.5rem;
  border: 1px solid #d9e3dc;
  border-radius: 1rem;
  color: #24332a;
  background: #f8faf8;
}
.card h2 { margin: 0 0 .75rem; }
.card p { margin: 0; line-height: 1.6; }

Compare this component with your notes, then add only the missing behavior. Use the font inspection guide for typography and the color palette workflow for reusable color roles.

7. Save decisions, not a property dump

Your final notes should name the component, its purpose, the source page, viewport, state, and properties that matter. Separate confirmed values from assumptions. A single screen cannot reveal every component variant or the rules used across an entire product.

For a broader audit, continue with extracting a design system from a website. Keep inspection evidence, implementation choices, and unresolved questions distinct so another developer can reproduce your reasoning.
imageAlt: A selected example button connects to CSS declarations for padding, border radius and background color.
coverAlt: A white add to chrome button with a blue inspection outline, dimension label and black cursor.

title: Turn Website Design Tokens into a Tailwind CSS v4 Theme
description: Map inspected colors and radii into semantic CSS variables and a Tailwind v4 theme, with an original example and component validation checklist.
body:
To turn website design tokens into a Tailwind CSS v4 theme, first identify recurring values and their roles, then map the values you have chosen for your project into Tailwind’s theme namespaces. Use ordinary CSS custom properties for semantic roles and @theme inline when Tailwind theme variables reference those properties.

The mapping is the easy part. The harder decision is which inspected values deserve to become shared rules. A page can contain one-off decoration, inherited defaults, and old overrides. Promoting every value into a token makes the theme harder to understand.

1. Collect values with their context

Before writing theme code, make a small inventory. For each candidate, record the component, visual role, state, and viewport. A green button background and a green success message may share a value while serving different purposes. Keep those roles separate even if they start with identical colors.

ObservationCandidate roleWhat to verify
Main content backgroundsurfaceOther pages and themes
Primary body textinkText on every surface
Primary action backgroundaccentHover and focus states
Repeated card roundingpanel radiusSmall and large cards

These are proposed names for an original implementation, not claims about how the inspected website names its tokens. Use the design-system extraction workflow to collect a broader sample before committing to a shared theme.

2. Choose semantic roles before utility names

Raw values describe appearance. Semantic roles describe intended use. A primitive might be green-900; a role might be ink. The distinction lets a theme change its appearance without changing what a component asks for.

For this tutorial, we will invent a compact reading interface with four roles: page surface, body text, accent, and text on the accent. Our values are examples, not extracted measurements or a claim that one palette suits every product. Validate the combinations in your own layout before shipping.

If you also exchange tokens between design tools, keep the interchange format separate from your Tailwind implementation. The Design Tokens Community Group format describes a JSON-based exchange format. A CSS theme file is not automatically a conforming token export.

3. Define the project’s CSS variables

Start with ordinary variables so components written without Tailwind can use the same decisions. Use a prefix that belongs to your project and avoid exporting every incidental measurement from the reference page.

:root {
  --site-surface: #f7faf7;
  --site-ink: #183224;
  --site-accent: #b9e8c7;
  --site-on-accent: #183224;
  --site-panel-radius: 1rem;
}

[data-theme="dark"] {
  --site-surface: #101b14;
  --site-ink: #ecf5ee;
  --site-accent: #b9e8c7;
  --site-on-accent: #183224;
}

Here, the dark theme changes the reading surface and text but keeps the action pairing. That is an intentional example decision. Do not infer an unseen dark theme from a light page. If a project has no approved dark palette, record that as an open design task.

4. Map the roles into Tailwind v4

In a project already configured for Tailwind CSS v4, add the following to the CSS entry file. The --color-* namespace supplies color utilities, and --radius-* supplies rounding utilities. Tailwind’s theme documentation recommends inline for theme values that reference other variables.

@import "tailwindcss";

@theme inline {
  --color-surface: var(--site-surface);
  --color-ink: var(--site-ink);
  --color-accent: var(--site-accent);
  --color-on-accent: var(--site-on-accent);
  --radius-panel: var(--site-panel-radius);
}

Place @import "tailwindcss"; first in the combined CSS entry file, followed by the earlier :root and dark-theme definitions and the @theme inline block. Now a component can request semantic utilities:

<article class="rounded-panel bg-surface p-6 text-ink">
  <h2 class="text-2xl font-semibold">A useful starting point</h2>
  <p class="mt-3 leading-relaxed">A small theme with clear roles.</p>
  <a href="/guides/" class="mt-6 inline-flex rounded-panel
    bg-accent px-4 py-3 text-on-accent
    focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-4">
    Explore the guides
  </a>
</article>

The code assumes your build scans the file containing these classes. It is a Tailwind v4 example; copying it into a v3 configuration does not perform an upgrade.

5. Add typography and spacing selectively

Only add a custom font family after the font files and loading strategy are part of your project. A family name in CSS does not install the font. Similarly, inspect several text roles before deciding a measured size represents a shared type scale.

Keep Tailwind’s existing spacing utilities when they fit the design. If your inventory shows a consistent alternative rhythm, document why it is necessary before replacing a global spacing decision. A single unusual gap is usually better handled locally than by redefining an entire scale.

6. Verify the theme through real components

Build a page containing a heading, paragraph, link, button, card, and input. This small specimen reveals missing roles more quickly than a palette displayed on its own. Test keyboard focus, long content, narrower widths, and every supported theme.

Use the palette inspection guide to review actual foreground/background pairings. Do not approve a color because its swatch looks pleasant. Check where the color appears and what the reader must distinguish.

7. Document what the theme guarantees

For each semantic role, write one sentence explaining when to use it. Add a short list of deliberate exceptions and unresolved observations. This prevents the next contributor from creating a new shade every time a screenshot looks slightly different.

Include those decisions in a DESIGN.md brief for an AI coding workflow if your team uses one. The goal is a small, explainable theme that supports real components, with clear evidence for the decisions you carried forward.
imageAlt: An observed accent color and spacing value are mapped to named Tailwind v4 theme variables and corresponding utility classes.
coverAlt: Tailwind v4 theme variables mapped to a site accent and panel radius, with matching utility chips.

title: DESIGN.md: A Practical Design Brief for AI Coding
description: Use this DESIGN.md template to give an AI coding assistant clear design tokens, layout rules, component states, evidence, and review criteria.
body:
A DESIGN.md file can serve as a human-readable design brief for an AI coding assistant: describe the interface, list approved design decisions, link relevant assets, and define how the result will be checked. In this guide, the filename is a suggested project convention. Do not assume every coding assistant automatically discovers it or treats it as a standardized instruction file.

The file works best when you explicitly provide it to the assistant and keep it close to the code it describes. A screenshot supplies visual context; the written brief explains which details are intentional, which interactions matter, and where the assistant should ask instead of inventing an answer.

1. Define the job and the audience

Start with the page’s purpose, the reader’s task, and the action the interface supports. “Build an elegant dashboard” leaves too many decisions open. “Build a project list where a team lead can identify overdue work and open a project” provides a useful basis for layout and behavior.

Name the stack and relevant files. Specify whether to reuse existing components, extend a theme, or create a new page. This keeps the work connected to your application.

2. Label evidence and assumptions

When you inspect a reference, record the URL, the date, viewport, and state. Identify what you directly observed and what you chose for your own implementation. A measured heading size does not prove the reference uses that size everywhere.

The website design-system extraction guide provides a useful starting inventory. Carry unresolved questions into the brief. For example, “mobile menu not observed” gives the builder a real constraint; silently inventing a menu and presenting it as faithful does not.

3. Start from this original template

The following is a complete example brief for a fictional project directory. Replace its choices with your approved decisions. The sample paths, colors, and widths describe that fictional implementation; they are not observations about another website.

# Design brief: Project directory

## Purpose
Help a team lead scan active projects and open the right one.
Primary action: open a project.
Secondary action: filter by status.

## Scope and implementation
Use the existing application framework and routing.
Reuse the project's Button and TextField components.
Keep the current project-loading and authentication behavior.
Implement the directory page, empty state, and filter state.

## Evidence
This brief defines an original design, not a website replica.
Reference assets: use only approved files in /assets/projects/.
Unknown: whether archived projects need a separate route.
Ask before adding an archive flow.

## Visual roles
Surface: #f7faf7
Primary text: #183224
Accent: #b9e8c7
Text on accent: #183224
Panel radius: 1rem
Use the existing font family and spacing scale.
Treat these as proposed values until contrast is checked.

## Layout
Place the page heading before filters and results.
Use a readable centered container with generous side padding.
At narrow widths, stack controls without clipping labels.
Let project titles wrap; do not hide essential status text.

## Components and behavior
Project item: title, owner, status, updated date, open link.
Filters: clear label, selected state, reset control.
Empty results: explain that no projects match; offer reset.
Loading: preserve layout and announce progress appropriately.
Error: explain the failed action and offer a retry.

## Accessibility and content
Use semantic headings and native controls where appropriate.
All actions must work with a keyboard and visible focus.
Do not use color as the only status cue.
Use realistic sample titles; do not invent customer claims.

## Review criteria
No horizontal page overflow at 375px or 1280px width.
Long titles and empty results remain usable.
Filters change visible results and reset restores them.
Verify contrast and keyboard navigation.
Report what was tested and any remaining limitations.

4. Link implementation data instead of duplicating it

If your project already has a theme file, point to it and explain the roles that matter. Copying a large token table into Markdown creates two places to update. A brief should make the source of truth obvious, especially when a color or type scale changes.

For Tailwind projects, see the guide to mapping design tokens into Tailwind v4. For interchange between tools, the Design Tokens Community Group format defines a structured token representation. This suggested Markdown brief complements those files; it does not replace their syntax or validation.

5. Ask the assistant to use the brief explicitly

Here is an original prompt you can adapt after placing the brief in your project:

Read DESIGN.md and the existing page, theme, and component files before editing. Implement the project directory described in the brief using the current stack. List any conflicting requirements or missing decisions first. Reuse existing components where they meet the requirements. After implementation, check the stated widths, keyboard interactions, filter reset, empty results, and long titles. Report the files changed, the checks performed, and unresolved limitations.

Replace generic references with actual paths. Keep the work small enough to review: one complete page with real states is a useful starting point.

6. Review the rendered result against the brief

Compare the implementation with the decisions in the file, not merely with its overall appearance. Verify that links go somewhere useful, controls operate, labels remain readable, and loading or empty states make sense. An attractive first screenshot can hide an unusable second state.

Use CSS inspection to investigate discrepancies. For responsive checks, Chrome’s device mode offers viewport simulation; confirm important mobile behavior on a real device as well. Record the tested conditions so a later reviewer knows what the result actually demonstrates.

7. Update decisions when the product changes

When an implementation reveals a better solution, update the brief alongside the code. Remove obsolete requirements rather than leaving contradictory instructions for the next pass. Keep a short change note for decisions whose reasoning would otherwise be lost.

The useful outcome is a repeatable collaboration: evidence becomes a brief, the brief guides an implementation, and the rendered implementation is checked against explicit criteria. The filename alone cannot provide that discipline; the quality of the decisions and the review does.
imageAlt: A DESIGN.md document organizes colors, typography, spacing and component states into an explicit brief for an AI coding tool.
coverAlt: A white DESIGN.md document window with a blue status dot and illustrative colors and typography sections.

title: Web Font Not Loading? A Chrome Debugging Checklist
description: Find why a web font falls back in Chrome. Check font requests, CSS paths, family names, weights and missing characters with a repeatable debugging workflow.
body:
When a web font does not load, first determine whether the browser requested the file, downloaded it successfully, and selected it for the text you are inspecting. These are separate checks. A successful download does not prove that a heading uses that face, and a font-family declaration does not prove that its first choice rendered.

Work on one visible heading or paragraph before changing the whole typography system. Keep its exact text, viewport and expected font weight in your notes. If the issue affects only one language or one weight, that narrow scope is valuable evidence.

1. Check the requested file before editing CSS

Open DevTools, select Network, enable Disable cache while DevTools is open, and reload. Filter for font requests. Inspect the URL, status and response headers of the relevant file. A missing request points toward a selection or stylesheet problem; a failed request points toward delivery. Chrome documents this workflow in its Network panel guide.

ObservationNext check
No matching requestIs the font-face rule loaded, and does visible text use its family?
404 responseDoes the deployed filename and letter case match the CSS URL?
200 response, wrong appearanceIs this a font response, and does the selected weight match?
Cross-origin errorCheck the font host’s allowed origin and the browser console.

A URL inside an external stylesheet is resolved relative to that stylesheet. For example, a stylesheet at /css/site.css with url("fonts/studio.woff2") requests /css/fonts/studio.woff2. If your file lives under /fonts/, use the correct relative path or a root-relative URL.

2. Align the family and face descriptors

Use a small, explicit rule to isolate the problem. This example assumes you own a real regular-weight file at the stated path; change the name and path to your project’s actual assets.

@font-face {
  font-family: "Studio Sans";
  src: url("/fonts/studio-sans-regular.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 400;
  font-style: normal;
  font-display: swap;
}
.article-copy {
  font-family: "Studio Sans", system-ui, sans-serif;
  font-weight: 400;
}

Do not label a static regular file as if it contains every weight. Add the correct bold face, or declare a supported weight range for a genuine variable font. The font-face reference explains the descriptors that match a file to a requested style.

3. Inspect the rendered face, not just the declaration

Select your test element and inspect its rendered fonts in Chrome’s Computed panel. A paragraph can use more than one font when the preferred face lacks a character. Test an ordinary word, accented text and any symbols involved in the bug. Our website font identification guide explains the distinction between the family list and the face actually drawn.

Temporarily set the element to weight 400 and normal style. If that works, restore the intended weight and compare. If the mismatch appears only immediately after navigation, investigate loading and fallback behavior before changing the chosen family. Adding more fallback names will not repair a broken font URL.

4. Verify the deployed fix

Save the change in source, rebuild and reload the public page with cache disabled. Confirm that the production response is the expected font and that the rendered-font panel identifies the intended face. Repeat on another browser or device when the defect was device-specific.

Record the failing request or mismatched descriptor alongside the fix. A useful completion note is “corrected the case-sensitive font filename and verified regular and bold text,” rather than “fonts fixed.” Keep the smallest reliable change; broad typography rewrites make the original cause harder to recognize later.
coverAlt: Illustrative font request panel with a missing file, a successful file and a rendered-font specimen.

title: How to Check Website Color Contrast, State by State
description: Audit text, buttons and focus indicators against their real backgrounds. Learn contrast thresholds, inspect transparent colors and record actionable fixes.
body:
To check website color contrast, measure the foreground against the background that actually appears behind it, then repeat for relevant states and themes. A palette of individually attractive colors tells you very little about whether a specific label is readable. The unit of review is the color pair in context.

Start with a page containing body text, secondary labels, links, inputs and buttons. Keep the viewport and theme fixed for the first pass. You can use the same recording format on later pages instead of collecting disconnected screenshots.

Choose the requirement that fits the element

WCAG’s minimum text contrast criterion uses 4.5:1 for ordinary text and 3:1 for large text. Large text means at least 18pt, or 14pt bold; those correspond to 24 CSS px and approximately 18.67 CSS px. A large button does not make its small label “large text.”

The non-text contrast criterion addresses visual information needed to identify controls, states and meaningful graphics, generally at 3:1 against adjacent colors. It does not mean every decorative card border needs that ratio. Disabled controls and other exceptions require their own interpretation; avoid treating one number as a complete accessibility verdict.

Build a pair inventory

Pair to inspectContext to retain
Body text / page surfaceSize, weight and reading area
Secondary label / card surfaceActual background beneath the label
Button label / button fillDefault, hover and pressed states
Focus indicator / adjacent surfaceLight and dark surfaces where it appears
Input boundary / surrounding surfaceWhether the boundary identifies the field

Open an element’s color value in DevTools and inspect the available contrast information. Record the CSS colors and the result, not a value sampled from an antialiased edge of a letter. If the tool cannot determine the background, inspect ancestor surfaces, overlays and opacity rather than assuming white.

Use a transparent-color example carefully

Suppose a secondary label uses 50% black on a white surface. The visible result is around mid-gray, not solid black. The same declaration over a gray card produces another pair. This is why copying only the foreground declaration from a reference can produce a different accessibility outcome in your implementation.

As a simple opaque reference, black on white has a 21:1 ratio. The illustrative pair #4A4A52 on #FFFFFF is approximately 8.48:1. A tool may display rounded values; do not round a result upward to decide whether it reaches a threshold. These examples are calculations, not measurements of a particular customer’s site.

Fix the role rather than one isolated pixel value

:root {
  --surface-card: #ffffff;
  --text-primary: #17191c;
  --text-secondary: #4a4a52;
}
.card {
  background: var(--surface-card);
  color: var(--text-primary);
}
.card .caption { color: var(--text-secondary); }

Treat this as a starter pair, then evaluate every place that uses the role. Darkening a shared secondary-text token can improve several components, but a role that also appears on colored banners may need a separate inverse variant. Keep that reasoning in the palette inventory.

Retest the states that are easy to miss

Tab through controls and check focus, activate hover where it exists, inspect validation errors, and repeat in dark mode. Look at text over gradients and images at several positions. A passing static label says nothing about a focus ring that disappears against the next surface.

Finish with an actionable issue record: page, element, state, foreground, background, measured ratio and proposed correction. Contrast is one accessibility check among many; also test keyboard operation, meaningful labels and layout when text grows. This small record lets another person reproduce your finding without guessing which version of a button you meant.
coverAlt: Two illustrative text and background pairs: dark gray on white at 8.48 to 1 and black on white at 21 to 1.

title: Why Your CSS Is Not Applying: Debug the Cascade
description: Find why a CSS declaration loses without adding random important flags. Trace selector matches, cascade layers, specificity, inheritance and source order.
body:
When CSS is not applying, inspect the winning declaration before making the selector more specific. Your rule might not match the element, might sit in an inactive media query, or might lose because of cascade layers or importance. Specificity is only one part of that decision.

Pick one property on one element: for example, the background of a primary button. Write down the expected value and the value shown in the Computed panel. This keeps a layout problem from becoming a general search through every stylesheet in the application.

Confirm the declaration can participate

In the Styles panel, look for your rule. If it is absent, confirm that the stylesheet loaded and the selector matches the selected element. If present but inactive, inspect its media or support condition. Check syntax warnings before assuming that the browser has ignored valid CSS.

A crossed-out declaration is useful evidence: another declaration won. Expand the property in Computed to trace its origin. If a shorthand is involved, inspect the corresponding longhand too. A later background declaration can reset details you set with a more specific-looking background property.

Read the cascade in the right order

MDN’s cascade explanation separates relevance, origin and importance, specificity, scoping proximity and order of appearance. Layer ordering also matters within an origin. Comparing selector weights before establishing which layer or importance level wins can lead to the wrong fix.

QuestionUseful evidence
Does the rule apply here?Selector match and active condition
Which precedence group wins?Origin, important flag and layer
Do selectors break the tie?Specificity of matching selectors
Is scope involved?Nearest applicable scope root
Is everything else equal?Order in the stylesheet

Reproduce a layered conflict

@layer components, overrides;

@layer components {
  .checkout .button.primary { background: navy; }
}
@layer overrides {
  .button { background: teal; }
}

For these normal author declarations, the later overrides layer wins even though its selector is less specific. Now imagine an unlayered normal .button rule elsewhere: unlayered normal styles take precedence over normal layered styles. Important declarations have different layer ordering, so do not extrapolate this example to every important rule.

The practical repair is often to put the intended override in the right place in the layer structure, rather than add an ID selector. Name layers once near the entry point and keep component ownership understandable. If a third-party library supplies styles, decide how it enters your cascade before fighting individual declarations.

Check inheritance separately

A color inherited from a parent is different from a declaration targeting the child. Even a highly specific parent rule does not automatically beat a rule applied directly to the child. Also check whether the property inherits at all. MDN’s specificity guide covers these distinctions.

For a concrete debugging note, record “child label has its own color rule” instead of “specificity too low.” That description points to the actual competing declaration. When a value comes from var(), follow the custom-property chain as a second step.

Make the smallest durable repair

Temporarily disable the winning declaration to confirm the diagnosis. Then change the source rule, layer placement or component API that should own the behavior. Re-enable the surrounding CSS and test another component using the same class. A local visual improvement can otherwise create an unintended global override.

Use !important only when its role is deliberate and documented, not as the first response to uncertainty. Save the final change in the project source; a successful edit in DevTools alone disappears when the page reloads. Check the default, focus and disabled variants before calling the component fixed.
coverAlt: Illustrative normal CSS layer comparison showing the overrides layer winning over a components layer.

title: CSS Grid vs Flexbox: Choose by the Layout You Need
description: Choose Grid or Flexbox using card alignment, wrapping and content behavior. Compare practical layouts, nested patterns and common sizing problems.
body:
Use Grid when items need shared rows and columns; use Flexbox when you primarily need to arrange and distribute items along one axis. A page often needs both: Grid for a card collection and Flexbox for the actions inside each card. Choose based on behavior, not on which syntax looks shorter.

Before rebuilding a reference, resize it and observe what changes. Do columns stay aligned across rows? Does the last row stretch? Do items follow their content width? A screenshot captures one arrangement but cannot tell you which constraints created it.

Compare a card collection with a toolbar

Layout requirementGood starting point
Cards share column boundaries across rowsGrid
Actions wrap according to their labelsFlexbox
Sidebar and main content have explicit tracksGrid
Icon and label align within one buttonFlexbox or inline-flex
A card grid contains flexible action rowsGrid outside, Flexbox inside

MDN’s comparison of Grid and other layouts explains the one-axis versus two-axis distinction. A wrapping flex container still lays out each line independently. If you need the last line to honor the same column tracks as earlier lines, Grid is usually the clearer starting point.

Build a responsive card grid

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns:
    repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 17rem), 1fr));
  gap: 1.5rem;
}
.card { min-width: 0; }

Here, 17rem is an example minimum comfortable card width, not a universal breakpoint. The inner minimum allows the track to fit a container narrower than that value. Available space determines the number of tracks, while fractional units distribute the remaining width. Try the actual content before accepting the chosen minimum.

Give three cards very different title lengths. Add a fourth and fifth card, then narrow the container. Check whether the final row behaves as intended and whether the card content can shrink. If a long URL pushes the track outward, investigate minimum sizing rather than immediately changing the column count.

Build a toolbar that follows its content

.toolbar {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-items: center;
  gap: .75rem;
}
.toolbar > .search {
  flex: 1 1 15rem;
  min-width: 0;
}

This pattern lets a search field claim flexible space while neighboring controls keep useful dimensions. Test the toolbar with translated or unusually long labels. If equal-width controls are a product requirement, express that requirement explicitly instead of relying on a convenient accidental distribution.

Keep visual order consistent with reading order

Avoid moving items visually merely to repair unsuitable source markup. A design can look correct while keyboard focus or reading order remains surprising. Start with a meaningful document order, then choose layout rules that preserve it. For a responsive sidebar, decide where its content belongs in the narrow reading sequence before assigning desktop tracks.

For nested layouts, write down which container owns each responsibility. The grid owns collection spacing and columns; the card owns its internal padding; the action row owns button alignment. This division makes later changes easier to locate than a single parent with many unrelated layout exceptions.

Use a short decision test

Render one item, several items and an incomplete final row. Replace the shortest label with a long one. Test a narrow container inside a wider page, since reusable components do not always receive the full viewport. If behavior breaks, classify the issue as track sizing, item minimum size, wrapping or content overflow.

Continue with the horizontal overflow checklist if the page becomes wider than the viewport. Use the spacing scale guide to keep gaps consistent after you have selected the correct layout behavior.
coverAlt: A grid diagram with shared columns beside a flex layout with independently sized items on each row.

title: How to Find and Fix Horizontal Overflow on Mobile
description: Track down the element making a page wider than its viewport. Fix grid minimums, long content, media and fixed widths without hiding useful content.
body:
To fix horizontal overflow, identify the box that exceeds its available width and correct that constraint. Hiding overflow on the entire page can conceal the symptom while leaving content, focus outlines or controls inaccessible. Start with the narrowest width that reproduces the problem.

Separate accidental page scrolling from intentional scrolling inside a code example or data table. A wide table may need its own scroll container. A paragraph or ordinary navigation bar generally should not push the whole document sideways.

Record the failing conditions

Use Chrome’s responsive viewport controls and change width gradually. Note the first width at which a horizontal scrollbar appears, the current page state, and whether a menu or dialog is open. Device mode approximates a mobile environment; verify the final behavior on a real device when possible.

Compare the problematic page with a simpler page that shares the same header. If both fail, inspect the shared shell first. If only a product page fails, examine its unique images, specifications and long names. This quick comparison reduces the number of containers you need to inspect.

Work from the widest box inward

Likely causeFocused repair
Fixed width exceeds the containerAdd an appropriate maximum width or responsive constraint
Flex or grid item refuses to shrinkInspect its automatic minimum size
Long unbroken URLAllow wrapping in the text region
Large image or videoConstrain media to its content container
Table or code blockProvide a deliberate local scrolling area

Use element highlights and the box-model panel to locate the edge extending beyond the viewport. Check padding and borders as well as the declared width. Also inspect absolute positioning and transforms: visual movement can create overflow even when the normal layout width seems reasonable.

Fix common constraints at their source

.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr);
}
.main, .card { min-width: 0; }
.article img, .article video {
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}
.long-link { overflow-wrap: anywhere; }
.code-scroll { max-width: 100%; overflow-x: auto; }

Apply each rule where its purpose fits. min-width: 0 allows a flex or grid item to shrink below an automatic content-based minimum; it does not magically wrap everything inside that item. MDN explains the automatic sizing behavior in its min-width reference.

If a two-column grid contains a sidebar and a wide article, use a track such as minmax(0, 1fr) for the flexible content and confirm that the sidebar also fits. On sufficiently narrow screens, the layout may need one column. Do not reduce text to an unreadable size merely to preserve the desktop arrangement.

Test content that stresses the layout

Replace a sample title with a long real title. Test an unbroken address, a large image, a multi-column table and enlarged text. Open the mobile menu and move keyboard focus through every item. A clipping fix that makes the screenshot look cleaner can still hide the currently focused control.

WCAG’s reflow guidance explains the goal of reading content without unnecessary scrolling in two dimensions, with exceptions for content whose meaning requires a two-dimensional layout. Use that distinction when deciding whether a local table scrollbar is appropriate.

Confirm the repair survives the full page

Reload after saving the source change, retest the original failing width and check widths on either side. Then inspect another page using the repaired component. Record the responsible selector and the content that exposed it so the next regression is reproducible.

A useful fix often removes one inappropriate width or minimum rather than adding many breakpoints. Once the page fits, return to spacing and typography; those decisions should improve readability within a working layout, not disguise an unresolved sizing constraint.
coverAlt: Illustrative mobile containers comparing an overflowing fixed-width card with a card constrained to the available width.

title: How to Build a CSS Spacing Scale from Real Components
description: Turn inconsistent margins, padding and gaps into a small CSS spacing scale. Audit component roles, handle exceptions and validate narrow layouts.
body:
A CSS spacing scale is a small set of reusable distances that helps components feel related. Build one by collecting actual gaps and padding, identifying repeated roles, and testing a proposed set against real content. An eight-pixel pattern can be useful, but it is a design choice rather than a rule every interface must obey.

Start with three components: a button, a card and a section containing several cards. Together they expose compact spacing, internal padding and larger layout rhythm. Include a narrow version of the page before deciding which values are permanent.

Separate the jobs that spacing performs

RoleExample observationQuestion
Control insetButton has 12px horizontal paddingDoes a longer label still fit?
Internal groupingCard title and description are 8px apartDo these elements read as one group?
Sibling separationCards have a 24px gapDoes the gap work after wrapping?
Section separationContent groups are 64px apartShould the distance reduce on mobile?

Record the value and its owner. A gap on a parent is different from margins on its children, even if a screenshot shows the same distance. MDN’s gap reference describes the property across grid, flex and multi-column layouts. Choose one owner for each repeated relationship so future changes do not accidentally double the space.

Propose a small primitive scale

:root {
  --space-1: .25rem;
  --space-2: .5rem;
  --space-3: .75rem;
  --space-4: 1rem;
  --space-6: 1.5rem;
  --space-8: 2rem;
  --space-12: 3rem;
}
.card { padding: var(--space-6); }
.card-stack { display: grid; gap: var(--space-3); }
.card-grid { display: grid; gap: var(--space-6); }

These are illustrative values. At a 16px root size, they correspond to 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32 and 48px. Keep the relative-unit relationship in mind when someone changes their text settings. Do not describe the values as fixed pixels if the implementation uses rem.

Numbers in token names can represent steps or multipliers; pick one convention and document it. Avoid silently switching between a literal pixel label and an arbitrary ordinal. A teammate should be able to predict what space-6 means without inspecting every component.

Add semantic roles only where they help

A role such as --card-padding can reference a primitive value and vary at a breakpoint. That is useful when the component has a stable purpose but different density. It is less useful to create dozens of aliases that merely restate one selector’s location.

Our design-system extraction guide recommends keeping observed values separate from proposed tokens. Use that same discipline here: a 22px gap in one reference does not prove that 22px belongs in the final scale. First check whether surrounding layout constraints produced it.

Keep exceptions visible

Optical alignment, borders and content-specific layouts can justify exceptions. A one-pixel icon adjustment is not necessarily a new spacing token. Record why it exists and keep it local to the component instead of distorting the entire scale to accommodate it.

Also inspect collapsed margins in ordinary block flow. If a measured vertical distance differs from the values you expected to add together, determine the layout behavior before renaming tokens. Replacing an uncertain margin relationship with an explicit parent gap may make intent easier to maintain, but verify the resulting layout rather than assuming equivalence.

Validate with a component sheet

Create a small page with the button, card and card collection using the proposed tokens. Test short and long content, multiple rows, narrow widths and enlarged text. Ask whether related elements remain close enough to read together and whether separate groups remain distinguishable.

Keep only values with a clear use. Deliver the token declarations, the component sheet and the few documented exceptions. A scale succeeds when it simplifies a real editing decision, such as increasing card padding consistently, rather than merely producing a neat sequence of numbers.
coverAlt: A spacing inventory with bars representing 8, 16, 24 and 32 pixel example distances.

title: Fluid Typography with CSS clamp(): A Worked Example
description: Create headings that scale between readable limits with CSS clamp. Calculate a fluid range, combine rem and viewport units, and test zoom behavior.
body:
CSS clamp() lets a font size grow between a minimum and maximum. Choose readable endpoint sizes first, calculate the expression between them, and test the result with real text and browser zoom. A mathematically smooth curve is not enough if the heading breaks its layout or stops responding well to user preferences.

This example builds a heading that measures 32px at a 400px viewport and 56px at a 1200px viewport under a 16px root-font assumption. Those dimensions are a worked design choice, not a recommended scale for every website.

Calculate the preferred value

The size difference is 24px across 800px of viewport width. The slope is 0.03, which becomes 3vw. To reach 32px at a 400px viewport, add a 20px intercept. Expressing the intercept and bounds in rem preserves a relationship with the root font size.

.hero-title {
  font-size: clamp(2rem, 1.25rem + 3vw, 3.5rem);
  line-height: 1.1;
  max-width: 18ch;
}
ViewportPreferred value at a 16px rootApplied size
320px29.6px32px minimum
400px32px32px
800px44px44px
1200px56px56px maximum
1440px63.2px56px maximum

If the root size changes, the rem terms change too, so these numeric endpoints shift. Treat the table as an explanation of one condition, not as a promise of exact sizes in every browser configuration. MDN’s clamp reference explains the minimum, preferred and maximum arguments.

Choose limits using content

Test the longest plausible heading, not only a short marketing phrase. Look for awkward single-word lines, overlap with nearby controls and excessive height on a small phone. A comfortable font size can still need a narrower line measure or a different layout.

The ch unit in the example provides a rough character-related measure based on the font’s zero glyph; it is not an exact character count. Compare the actual typeface. Two fonts at the same CSS size and width can produce noticeably different line breaks.

Keep body text decisions separate

A large display heading can benefit from substantial variation, while body text may need a much narrower range or no fluid scaling. Start body copy at a readable size with an appropriate line height. Avoid shrinking paragraphs solely to preserve a desktop composition on mobile.

Use a small set of role tokens if several headings share the pattern. For example, keep one display size and one section-title size instead of assigning an unrelated clamp expression to every component. That gives the next designer a few understandable controls rather than a page full of independent curves.

Test zoom and user text settings

Combining rem and viewport units does not automatically guarantee accessible resizing. Browser zoom changes the effective CSS viewport as well as text rendering, which can counteract some viewport-based growth. Test 200% zoom, increased default font size, and narrow reflow with the actual page.

WCAG’s resize-text guidance focuses on allowing text to enlarge without losing content or functionality. Check that buttons, cards and navigation can grow with the text. If a particular clamp range prevents sufficient resizing, revise the expression or use a simpler relative size.

Document the intended behavior

Record the two endpoint assumptions, the font family, line height and line measure alongside the token. Include a screenshot at the narrow, middle and wide widths and a note about the zoom checks you performed. That is more useful than handing over an unexplained formula.

If text still looks wrong, confirm the rendered font with the font inspection workflow. If it extends beyond its container, use the overflow guide to diagnose the layout instead of repeatedly reducing the font size.
coverAlt: Three typography specimens increasing from 32 to 44 to 56 pixels with the example fluid clamp expression.

title: How to Inspect and Rebuild a CSS Box Shadow
description: Read CSS shadow layers, offsets, blur and spread. Rebuild subtle card elevation, identify clipping, and test the result on the intended background.
body:
To rebuild a CSS box shadow, inspect the full computed value, separate its layers, and compare the result on the same kind of background. A soft shadow sampled from a screenshot can be difficult to distinguish from a border, gradient or second layer. Start with the actual declaration when the page is available.

Select the component itself, then inspect its wrapper and pseudo-elements if the visible effect is missing from its styles. The outer wrapper may own the elevation while an inner element clips media to rounded corners. Knowing which element owns the effect prevents a fragile recreation.

Read the numbers in order

.panel {
  box-shadow:
    0 1px 2px 0 rgb(16 16 19 / 8%),
    0 12px 28px -8px rgb(16 16 19 / 18%);
}

Within each layer, the length values represent horizontal offset, vertical offset, blur radius and optional spread radius. The color controls the shadow’s appearance; inset changes it to an inner shadow. Commas separate layers. The box-shadow reference documents the syntax and painting behavior.

Part of this exampleVisual intention
0 horizontal offsetKeep the shadow centered horizontally
Small first-layer offset and blurSuggest contact near the panel edge
Larger second-layer blurAdd a softer surrounding lift
Negative spread on the second layerPull that layer inward before blurring

These values are an original starting example, not an extracted recipe for a specific product. The distinction matters when your goal is to understand a reference: record the original declaration separately from the adjustments you choose for your own interface.

Isolate one layer at a time

Temporarily remove the second shadow and inspect the edge at normal viewing size. Then restore it and remove the first. This reveals whether the component depends on a crisp contact cue, a broad halo or both. Change one parameter at a time so you can identify what caused the improvement.

Keep the card background and surrounding surface visible. A shadow tuned on pure white can feel heavy on pale gray, and a dark surface may need a border or lighter separation rather than a stronger black blur. Do not compare isolated transparent previews as if they were complete page contexts.

Check clipping and ownership

If the shadow disappears along one edge, inspect ancestors for overflow clipping. Adding more blur will not restore a portion that a parent cuts away. Consider separating the element that casts the shadow from the element that clips its contents.

.card-shell {
  border-radius: 1rem;
  box-shadow: 0 8px 24px rgb(16 16 19 / 12%);
}
.card-media {
  border-radius: 1rem 1rem 0 0;
  overflow: hidden;
}

This pattern gives the outer shell responsibility for elevation and the media region responsibility for image clipping. It is only appropriate when those responsibilities match your component. Check focus outlines and menus too: clipping that works for a photograph may be wrong for an interactive child.

Name the role after the decision

A token such as --shadow-floating-panel communicates where the effect belongs. A token named after every numeric detail becomes awkward as soon as the values change. Keep a small elevation set and show each role on the actual page surfaces used by your product.

Avoid using decorative shadow alone to communicate an essential control boundary or state. Pair the effect with a clear structure and verify relevant contrast. For a dark theme, review semantic surface tokens rather than applying a global inversion filter.

Validate the complete component

Check the default and hover states at narrow and wide sizes. Inspect a dense group of cards, where overlapping shadows can make the page look muddy, and a floating panel near a viewport edge. Finally, save the values in source and verify the deployed version. The goal is a stable elevation role that supports the component, not a shadow that looks impressive only in isolation.
coverAlt: A layered card elevation illustration labeling a contact shadow and a softer surrounding shadow.

title: Build a Consistent Border Radius System in CSS
description: Choose useful radius tokens for buttons, cards and nested surfaces. Inspect real corners, avoid clipping focus rings, and document intentional exceptions.
body:
A border radius system gives repeated components a consistent shape without forcing every object to have identical corners. Start with a few roles, such as controls, cards and floating panels, then test them at their actual dimensions. A 12px radius looks very different on a small input and a large content card.

Inspect the computed corner values of a reference rather than estimating from a scaled screenshot. Record the component width and height too. If the value is a percentage, the apparent curve can change when the box changes size.

Identify the shape, not just the number

The border-radius reference explains circular and elliptical corners, individual corner values and percentage behavior. Check whether the component uses one value for all corners, separate horizontal and vertical radii, or individual corner overrides.

Shape roleExample starting valueCheck
Compact field0.5remDoes the curve crowd the label or icon?
Content card1remDoes it match the card’s size and padding?
Floating panel1.25remDoes it feel related to the cards?
Pill control999pxDoes it stay comfortable when its label wraps?

These example values are a proposed system, not an industry standard. Compare a small set on a component sheet and choose the set that suits your product. If each component requires a slightly different value, review whether its dimensions or spacing are inconsistent before adding another token.

Create named roles

:root {
  --radius-control: .5rem;
  --radius-card: 1rem;
  --radius-panel: 1.25rem;
  --radius-pill: 999px;
}
.field { border-radius: var(--radius-control); }
.card { border-radius: var(--radius-card); }
.dialog { border-radius: var(--radius-panel); }

Keep shape and spacing separate even when they happen to share a number. Increasing card padding should not unexpectedly change input corners. A shared primitive scale can support both, but role aliases should make each design decision explicit.

Treat nested corners as a geometry problem

An inner rounded surface with the same radius as its outer container can produce uneven-looking corner spacing. As a starting approximation for evenly inset circular curves, reduce the inner radius by the inset. For a 24px outer radius and an 8px inset, try a 16px inner radius, then inspect the result.

That subtraction is a design starting point, not a universal CSS formula. Borders, unequal padding and elliptical corners complicate the relationship. Test the real component instead of globally applying a calculation to every nested element.

Separate rounding from clipping

Rounded borders do not automatically solve every child-content clipping problem. An image may need a matching radius or a dedicated clipping wrapper. Before adding overflow: hidden to the entire card, check whether it contains focus outlines, menus or tooltips that should extend beyond the edge.

For media cards, let the media region handle image clipping and leave the interactive shell free to show its focus treatment. The shadow guide uses a similar separation between the element that clips content and the element that casts elevation.

Review awkward states

Test long button labels, multi-line inputs, a card with no image and a card with a full-width image. Check narrow layouts and enlarged text. A pill that looks balanced with a single word may become a large capsule when its label wraps; decide whether that is acceptable or whether the component needs another shape role.

Record any asymmetric corners as intentional component behavior. For example, a grouped control may square off adjoining edges while preserving the outer corners. Do not add unexplained overrides simply to match one screenshot.

Finish with a small radius table, representative component examples and a list of exceptions. Link it to your spacing decisions so later edits preserve the relationship between a component’s outline and the content inside it.
coverAlt: Three white component shapes illustrating an 8 pixel control radius, a 16 pixel card radius and a pill.

title: CSS Variable Fallbacks: Missing Values vs Invalid Values
description: Debug CSS custom properties by tracing scope, inheritance and var fallbacks. Learn why an existing value of the wrong type can still break a declaration.
body:
A var() fallback helps when the referenced custom property is missing or has an invalid custom-property value. It does not validate every value against the property where you use it. If --text-color exists but contains 20px, inserting it into color can invalidate the declaration instead of choosing your fallback color.

When a token appears to do nothing, inspect the consuming property and then follow the custom property through its scope. This is more reliable than repeatedly adding fallback arguments without checking which value the browser receives.

Start with a missing token

.notice {
  color: var(--notice-text, #243449);
  background: var(--notice-surface, #edf3fa);
}

In this unregistered-variable example, absent notice tokens allow the supplied values to be used. The fallback belongs to that individual use of the variable; it does not define the token for other components. If several components need the same default, a declaration on an appropriate shared ancestor may be easier to maintain.

Compare a value of the wrong type

.example {
  --text-color: 20px;
  color: var(--text-color, #243449);
}

The custom property exists, so the fallback is not selected merely because 20px is unsuitable as a color. After substitution, the color declaration is invalid at computed-value time. For an inherited property such as color, that can result in inherited color rather than the earlier declaration you expected. MDN explains this distinction in its custom properties guide.

SymptomCheck first
Fallback appears unexpectedlyIs the token in scope on this element?
Neither intended value nor fallback appearsIs the substituted value valid for the consuming property?
Child differs from parentIs there a local override or registration changing inheritance?
Only one theme breaksDoes that theme define every required semantic token?

Trace scope and spelling

Custom-property names are case-sensitive. Compare the exact name in the definition and use, including prefixes. Next inspect the selected element’s ancestors and any local override. A token defined inside a sibling component is not a global variable for the rest of the document.

In DevTools, expand the consuming property and follow the value to its declaration. Temporarily replace the variable with a known valid literal. If the property still does not take effect, return to the cascade debugging guide; the variable may not be the cause.

Use registration when a typed token helps

@property --notice-text {
  syntax: "<color>";
  inherits: true;
  initial-value: #243449;
}

Registration declares a type, an inheritance rule and an initial value. This changes how the token behaves compared with an unregistered custom property. The property registration reference describes the required descriptors and validity conditions. Check support in your target browsers before depending on registered behavior.

Choose inherits deliberately. Theme tokens often need to flow to descendants, while a component’s internal animated value might not. Do not copy a registration with inheritance disabled into a theme system and then assume every child receives the parent’s override.

Make the token contract explicit

Document the expected type, where the token is defined, whether it inherits and which components consume it. For a color role, include the paired surface rather than only a hex value. For a spacing role, state whether percentages are permitted or whether it should always be a length.

Test the normal value, a missing value and a deliberately incorrect value in a small local example. Those three cases reveal different failure modes. Once the contract is clear, map the reviewed tokens into your framework using the Tailwind theme workflow rather than exporting an unexamined pile of custom properties.
coverAlt: A variable debugging diagram distinguishing a missing token using its fallback from an existing length used incorrectly as a color.

title: Build Dark Mode with Semantic CSS Color Tokens
description: Create light and dark themes with semantic CSS variables. Respect system preferences, distinguish color-scheme, and test surfaces, controls and contrast.
body:
Build dark mode by assigning new values to semantic color roles, not by inverting the finished page. Text, surfaces, borders and actions have different jobs. A role-based theme lets a component keep its meaning while its values change between light and dark contexts.

Start with one complete component and its surrounding page surface. Include a label, secondary text, a button, a border and a focus state. Testing only a blank dark canvas misses most of the decisions that make a theme usable.

Define roles before shades

RoleQuestion to answer
Page surfaceWhat sits behind the main content?
Raised surfaceHow does a card separate from the page?
Primary textWhat color carries the main reading content?
Secondary textDoes supporting copy remain readable?
Action and focusHow are interaction and keyboard position visible?

Avoid naming a role after its current appearance, such as white-card, when that appearance will change. A name such as surface-card survives both themes. Keep brand accents separate from text-on-accent colors; a brand color does not guarantee that either white or black text will pass contrast.

Implement a system-preference version

:root {
  color-scheme: light;
  --surface-page: #f5f5f5;
  --surface-card: #ffffff;
  --text-primary: #17191c;
  --text-secondary: #4a4a52;
  --border-card: #d6d5d7;
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --surface-page: #101013;
    --surface-card: #1c1c21;
    --text-primary: #f4f4ee;
    --text-secondary: #c4c4cc;
    --border-card: #45454e;
  }
}
body { background: var(--surface-page); color: var(--text-primary); }
.card {
  background: var(--surface-card);
  border: 1px solid var(--border-card);
}
.caption { color: var(--text-secondary); }

The prefers-color-scheme media feature detects the user’s requested theme. The separate color-scheme property informs browser-provided rendering such as form controls and scrollbars. It does not automatically redesign every authored element.

This example follows the system preference only. A user-selectable light, dark and system control requires additional state and precedence rules. If you add one, make the explicit choice override the system setting and decide how that choice persists. Do not describe a system-only media query as a complete theme toggle.

Review assets and elevated surfaces

A transparent logo that looks clear on white may disappear on a dark card. Test logos, charts and illustrations against their actual destination surfaces. For complex images, provide an intentional background or a suitable alternate asset instead of applying a blanket inversion filter.

Shadows also need review. Increasing black shadow opacity on a nearly black background may provide little useful separation. A lighter card surface, border or different elevation treatment can be more effective. The shadow inspection guide shows how to separate those effects.

Audit pairs and states in each theme
